'''Dame Carol Vivien Robinson'''  {{post-nominals|DBE|FRS|FMedSci}} (born 10 April 1956) is a British [[chemist]] and former president of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] (2018–2020).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/carol-robinson-12181/|title=Carol Robinson profile|website=royalsociety.org|language=en-gb|access-date=4 August 2019}}</ref> She was a [[Royal Society]] Research Professor and is the [[Dr Lee's Professorships|Dr Lee's Professor]] of Physical and Theoretical Chemistry, and a professorial fellow at [[Exeter College, Oxford|Exeter College]], [[University of Oxford]]. She is the founding director of the Kavli Institute for Nanoscience Discovery, University of Oxford,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Home |url=https://kavli.web.ox.ac.uk/about-us |access-date=10 June 2022 |website=www.kavlinano.ox.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref> and she was previously professor of [[mass spectrometry]] at the chemistry department of the [[University of Cambridge]].<ref name="caredit">{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1126/science.caredit.a1100023| title = An Interview with Carol Robinson| journal = Science| year = 2011| last1 = Pain | first1 = Elisabeth}}</ref><ref name="thelifescientific">{{cite web|url=http://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b049yhcn|title= Carol Robinson interviewed on The Life Scientific|year=2014|first=Jim|last=Al-Khalili|website=bbc.co.uk|publisher=[[BBC]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1038/476273a| pmid = 21850083| title = Women in science: In pursuit of female chemists| journal = Nature| volume = 476| issue = 7360| pages = 273–5| year = 2011| last1 = Robinson | first1 = C. V. | author-link1 = Carol V. Robinson|bibcode = 2011Natur.476..273R | s2cid = 205066711| doi-access = free}}</ref><ref>{{Scopus id}}</ref><ref name=official>Carol Robinson's {{Official website}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Born in Kent, the daughter of Denis E. Bradley and Lillian (née Holder),<ref name=freebmd>{{Cite web|url=http://www.freebmd.org.uk/cgi/information.pl?cite=85JTjI84DFI0qLhrykp6ZA&scan=1|title=Births June 1956: Index entry|access-date=23 July 2014|work=FreeBMD|publisher=ONS}}</ref> Carol Vivien Bradley left school at 16 and began her career as a lab technician in [[Sandwich, Kent]] with [[Pfizer]], where she began working with the then novel technique of [[mass spectrometry]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ft.com/content/fdc185f6-7bb2-11e4-a695-00144feabdc0|title=Dame Carol Robinson: from school leaver at 16 to leading chemist|last=Sullivan|first=Ruth|date=12 December 2014|website=Financial Times|issn=0307-1766|access-date=5 August 2016}}</ref>

Her potential was spotted, and she gained further qualifications at evening classes and day release from her job at [[Pfizer]]. After earning her degree, she left Pfizer and studied for a Master of Science degree at the [[University of Swansea]], followed by a Ph.D. at the [[University of Cambridge]],<ref name="phd">{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|first=Carol Vivien|last=Bradley|title=Structural studies on bioactive organic compounds|publisher=University of Cambridge|year=1982|url=http://ulmss-newton.lib.cam.ac.uk/vwebv/holdingsInfo?bibId=6374|id={{EThOS|uk.bl.ethos.350044}}|website=lib.cam.ac.uk|author-link=Carol V. Robinson|archive-date=6 July 2020|access-date=29 November 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200706113858/https://ulmss-newton.lib.cam.ac.uk/vwebv/holdingsInfo?bibId=6374|url-status=dead}}</ref> which she completed in just two years.<ref name="thelifescientific"/> During this time she was a student at [[Churchill College, Cambridge]].<ref name=whoswho/>

==Career and research==
After a [[postdoctoral research|postdoctoral]] training fellowship at the [[University of Bristol]],<ref name=bristol>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141118134813/http://www.bristol.ac.uk/pace/graduation/honorary-degrees/hondeg13/robinson.html|url=http://www.bristol.ac.uk/pace/graduation/honorary-degrees/hondeg13/robinson.html|publisher=University of Bristol|title=Professor Dame Carol Robinson, FRS, Doctor of Science, 15 July 2013|archive-date=18 November 2014}}</ref> Robinson took up a junior position in the [[mass spectrometry]] unit at the [[University of Oxford]], where she began analysing [[protein folding]].<ref name=doyenne>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/education/2004/jun/22/highereducationprofile.highereducation|title=Carol Robinson: Society doyenne|newspaper=[[The Guardian]]|date=22 June 2004|first=John|last=Crace|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140302144724/http://www.theguardian.com/education/2004/jun/22/highereducationprofile.highereducation|archive-date=2 March 2014}}</ref> Robinson and colleagues successfully captured protein folding in the presence of the [[Chaperone (protein)|chaperone]] [[GroEL]], demonstrating that at least some aspects of protein secondary structure could be studied in the [[Phase (matter)|gas phase]].

Robinson was the first woman professor in the department of chemistry at both the [[University of Cambridge]] (2001) and the [[University of Oxford]] (2009).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://robinsonweb.chem.ox.ac.uk/carol-robinson.aspx|title=Carol Robinson Profile|publisher=University of Oxford|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140305200539/http://robinsonweb.chem.ox.ac.uk/carol-robinson.aspx|archive-date=5 March 2014}}</ref>{{independent source inline|date=December 2024}} Her research demonstrated that [[electrospray ionization]] mass spectrometry could be used to study [[protein]]s and other complex [[macromolecule]]s in the gas phase.<ref name="rsocbio">{{Cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/carol-robinson-12181/|title=Carol Robinson|website=royalsociety.org|language=en-gb|access-date=24 November 2017}}</ref> In addition to her contributions to the study of protein folding, Robinson has studied [[ribosome]]s, [[Chaperone (protein)|molecular chaperones]] and most recently [[membrane protein]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal

T.|bibcode = 2005Sci...310.1658R| pmid=16293722| s2cid = 37135092}}</ref> Her research has made contributions to gas-phase structural biology, including the study of protein complexes in their native environments for drug discovery.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Viegas|first=Jennifer|date=16 April 2019|title=Profile of Dame Carol Robinson|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=116|issue=16|pages=7608–7610|doi=10.1073/pnas.1903862116|issn=0027-8424|pmid=30936318|pmc=6475430|bibcode=2019PNAS..116.7608V |doi-access=free}}</ref> Additionally, she is a co-founder of OMass Therapeutics, a [[University of Oxford]] spin-out company applying mass spectrometry technology to drug discovery.<ref>{{cite web |title=Get to know About Us |url=https://www.omass.com/team/#ourfounders |access-date=7 March 2020 |website=OMass}}</ref>

==Honours and awards==
Robinson was awarded the [[American Society for Mass Spectrometry]]'s Biemann Medal in 2003, and the [[Christian B. Anfinsen#Christian B. Anfinsen Award|Christian B. Anfinsen Award]] in 2008. In 2004, the [[Royal Society]] awarded her both a [[Fellow of the Royal Society|Fellowship (FRS)]]<ref name="royal"/> and the [[Rosalind Franklin Award]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://royalsociety.org/events/2004/rare-gases-ribosomes|title=Finding the right balance: from rare gases to ribosomes|website=royalsociety.org|publisher=The Royal Society|date=15 November 2004|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140810154637/https://royalsociety.org/events/2004/rare-gases-ribosomes/|archive-date=10 August 2014}}</ref> Her citation for the Royal Society reads:<ref name="royal">{{cite web |url=http://royalsociety.org |title=EC/2004/37: Robinson, Carol Vivien |author=Anon |year=2004 |publisher=The Royal Society |archive-date=10 July 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190710033907/https://collections.royalsociety.org/DServe.exe?dsqIni=Dserve.ini&dsqApp=Archive&dsqDb=Catalog&dsqCmd=show.tcl&dsqSearch=%28RefNo%3D%3D%27EC%2F2004%2F37%27%29 |location=London |url-status=dead |access-date=24 July 2008 }}</ref>

<blockquote>Distinguished for her research on the application of mass spectrometry to problems in [[chemical biology]]. She has used mass spectrometry to define the folding and binding of interacting [[Multiprotein complex|proteins in large complexes]]. Most importantly, she has established that macromolecular complexes such as [[GroEL]], [[ribosome]]s, and intact virus [[capsid]]s can be generated in the gas phase and their [[electrospray]] mass spectra recorded. This work has demonstrated the power of mass spectrometry in studying very large complexes and allowed her to define changes in their conformation and the manner of their assembly.</blockquote>

She was elected a [[Fellow of the Academy of Medical Sciences]] in 2009.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Professor Dame Carol Robinson DBE FRS FMedSci |url=https://acmedsci.ac.uk/fellows/fellows-directory/ordinary-fellows/fellow/Carol%20Vivien-Robinson-0033z00002qIIgHAAW |access-date=2026-06-14 |website=Academy of Medical Sciences}}</ref>

In 2010, Robinson received the [[Davy Medal]] "for her ground-breaking and novel use of mass spectrometry for the characterisation of large protein complexes".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://royalsociety.org/Davy-Medal|title=The Davy Medal (1877)|publisher=The Royal Society|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150316083902/https://royalsociety.org/awards/davy-medal/|archive-date=16 March 2015}}</ref><ref name="bieman">{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1016/j.jasms.2004.07.011| pmid = 15465349| title = Focus in honor of Carol V. Robinson, 2003 Biemann Medal awardee| journal = Journal of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry| volume = 15| issue = 10| pages = 1379–1381| year = 2004| last1 = Loo | first1 = J. A. | last2 = Gross | first2 = M. L. | doi-access = free| bibcode = 2004JASMS..15.1379L}}</ref>

In 2011, she was given the Interdisciplinary Prize by the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] for "development of a new area of research, gas-phase structural biology, using highly refined mass spectrometry techniques",<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.rsc.org/prizes-funding/prizes/find-a-prize/interdisciplinary-prizes/|title=Interdisciplinary Prizes|website=Royal Society of Chemistry|accessdate=18 March 2022}}</ref> the [[Aston Medal]], and the [[FEBS]]/[[European Molecular Biology Organization|EMBO]] [[FEBS/EMBO Women in Science Award|Women in Science Award]].

She was appointed [[Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire]] (DBE) in the [[2013 New Year Honours]] for services to science and industry.<ref>Anon (2012) {{London Gazette|issue=60367|date=29 December 2012|page=7 |supp=y}}</ref>

She received the [[International Mass Spectrometry Foundation|Thomson Medal Award]] in 2014.<ref>{{Cite web  | title = The 2014 Thomson Medal Award IMSC 2014 | url = http://www.imsc2014.ch/?page_id=46 | access-date = 8 April 2014 }}</ref>

In 2015, she was a laureate of the L'Oréal-UNESCO For Women in Science Awards "for her groundbreaking work in macromolecular mass spectrometry and pioneering gas phase structural biology by probing the structure and reactivity of single proteins and protein complexes, including membrane proteins."<ref>{{Cite web |title=2015 Awards {{!}} United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization |url=http://www.unesco.org/new/en/natural-sciences/priority-areas/gender-and-science/for-women-in-science-programme/2015-awards/ |access-date=11 September 2023 |website=wayback.archive-it.org |archive-date=7 July 2018 |archive-url=https://wayback.archive-it.org/10611/20180707004705/http://www.unesco.org/new/en/natural-sciences/priority-areas/gender-and-science/for-women-in-science-programme/2015-awards/ |url-status=bot: unknown }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=L’ORÉAL-UNESCO - FOR WOMEN IN SCIENCE - 2015 LAUREATE - Europe - Professor Dame Carol Robinson - Physical Chemistry & Mass Spectrometry | url=https://www.fondationloreal.com/sites/default/files/2020-12/2015%20L%27Or%C3%A9al%20UNESCO%20For%20Women%20in%20Science.pdf | website=Fondation L'Oreal | page=19 | access-date=2026-04-11}}</ref>

In 2017, she was elected a Foreign Associate of the US [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="FANAS">{{cite web |url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/may-2-2017-NAS-Election.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170503160816/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/may-2-2017-NAS-Election.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=3 May 2017 |title=News from the National Academy of Sciences|website=nasonline.org |publisher=[[National Academy of Sciences]] |date=2 May 2017 |access-date=3 May 2017 }}</ref>

In 2018, she won the Frank H. Field and Joe L. Franklin Award for Outstanding Achievement in Mass Spectrometry from the [[American Chemical Society]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/frank-h-field-and-joe-l-franklin-award-for-outstanding-achievement-in-mass-spectrometry.html|title=Frank H. Field and Joe L. Franklin Award|website=acs.org|publisher= ACS}}</ref>

In 2019, she won the [[Novozymes Prize]] for "almost single-handedly founding a subfield of mass spectrometry proteomics".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://novonordiskfonden.dk/en/news/prize-recipient-made-proteins-float-in-soap-bubbles/|title=Prize recipient made proteins float in soap bubbles|website=Novo Nordisk Fonden|language=en-US|access-date=25 February 2019}}</ref> Also in 2019 she received the [[Royal Medal]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/grants-schemes-awards/awards/royal-medal/|title=Royal Medals &#124; Royal Society|website=royalsociety.org|date=22 February 2019|access-date=18 March 2022}}</ref>

In 2020, she was chosen as the recipient of the [[Othmer Gold Medal]].<ref name="Othmer">{{cite web|title=Othmer Gold Medal|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/othmer-gold-medal|publisher=[[Science History Institute]]|access-date=1 February 2018|date=31 May 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=2022 Louis-Jeantet Prize for Professor Dame Carol Robinson|date=30 November 2021|website=Department of Chemistry, University of Oxford|url=https://www.chem.ox.ac.uk/article/2022-louis-jeantet-prize-for-professor-dame-carol-robinson}}</ref>

In 2021, she received the 2022 [[Louis-Jeantet Prize for Medicine]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Carol Robinson wins 2022 Louis-Jeantet Prize|date=November 2021|website=The Vallee Foundation|url=https://thevalleefoundation.org/news/carol-robinson-wins-2022-louis-jeantet-prize}}</ref> and the 2022 European Chemistry Gold Medal by the [[European Chemical Society]].<ref name="EuChemS 2021">{{cite web | title=2022 European Chemistry Gold Medal awarded to Professor Dame Carol Robinson | website=EuChemS | date=24 August 2021 | url=https://www.euchems.eu/2022-gold-medal/ | access-date=18 March 2022}}</ref> Also in 2021, she became an International Honorary Member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Carol V. Robinson |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/carol-v-robinson |access-date=10 June 2022 |website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences |language=en}}</ref>

In 2022, she was awarded the [[Franklin Institute Awards|Franklin Institute Award]] for Chemistry.<ref>{{Cite web |date=23 November 2021 |title=Carol V. Robinson |url=https://www.fi.edu/laureates/carol-v-robinson |access-date=10 June 2022 |website=The Franklin Institute |language=en}}</ref>

In 2023, she was elected to the American Philosophical Society and was awarded the John B. Fenn Award for Distinguished Contribution to Mass Spectrometry.<ref>{{Cite web |date=22 June 2023 |title=Carol V. Robinson |url=https://www.asms.org/about-asms-awards/distinguished-contribution|access-date=22 June 2023 |website=American Society for Mass Spectrometry|language=en}}</ref> She was named one of the top ten "Innovators and Trailbalzers" on the 2023 Power List by the Analytical Scientist.<ref>{{Cite web |date=10 September 2023 |title=The Power List 2023 |url=https://theanalyticalscientist.com/power-list/2023 |access-date=2 September 2023 |website=The Analytical Scientist |language=en}}</ref>

In 2024, she received the EPO European Inventor Lifetime Achievement Award for her work in mass spectrometry that  significantly advanced biochemical research and medical diagnostics. On 19 June 2024, she received an honorary doctorate from the University of Cambridge in recognition of her achievements in chemistry.

In 2024, she was inducted into the National Academy of Inventors.

She has been awarded 13 honorary doctorates including the Weizmann Institute of Science, Aarhus University Denmark, [[University of Kent]], the [[University of York]], and the [[University of Bristol]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=About Carol |url=https://robinsonweb.chem.ox.ac.uk/about-carol |access-date=11 September 2023 |website=robinsonweb.chem.ox.ac.uk |language=en}}</ref>

On 10 August 2025, Robinson appeared on [[BBC Radio 4]]'s ''[[Desert Island Discs]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.exeter.ox.ac.uk/exeter-fellow-professor-dame-carol-robinson-to-feature-on-bbc-radio%E2%80%AF4s-desert-island-discs/|title=Exeter Fellow Professor Dame Carol Robinson to feature on BBC Radio 4's Desert Island Discs|website=exeter.ox.ac.uk|publisher=Exeter College Oxford|date=5 August 2025|access-date=10 August 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/m002gzqj|title=Desert Island Discs {{!}} Professor Dame Carol Robinson, scientist|website=bbc.co.uk|publisher=BBC Radio 4|date=10 August 2025}}</ref>
